opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that when people edit an image, they almost always have a very specific intent. They want to change one thing, maybe relight the scene, remove an object, change someone's expression, and they want everything else to stay exactly as it was. That's really the difference between editing and generation. With generation you're happy to get any plausible image that matches a prompt. With editing, the input image is the most important constraint you have, because it carries the details the user cares about: the identity of a person, the texture of a fabric, the exact composition they chose when they took the photo.

What we've seen with a lot of generative approaches is that they're very good at producing something that looks realistic, but they tend to drift. You invert the image into the model's latent space, make your change, and when you come back out the face looks a little different, the background has subtly shifted, fine details like text or patterns get hallucinated. Each change on its own might look small, but people are incredibly sensitive to it, especially with faces or photos that matter to them personally. If the person in the edited photo doesn't quite look like your friend anymore, the edit has failed, however good the image looks.

So for me, high fidelity really means two things together: the edit you asked for should be done convincingly, and everything you didn't ask to change should be preserved as closely as possible, ideally down to the pixel level where that makes sense. A lot of the interesting technical work is in managing that tradeoff. You want to use the strong priors in these generative models to fill in plausible content, but without letting those priors overwrite what's actually in the photo. Professionals especially won't adopt a tool that quietly changes their image in ways they didn't ask for. Trust is a big part of it. If you can't rely on the tool to respect your input, you end up spending more time fixing its side effects than you saved.

r001.rationale: The response says that even a slight change to a face can make the person look different and cause the edit to fail, clearly linking facial drift to loss of identity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to frame it is that when someone comes to an editing tool, they already have an image they care about. They're not asking for a new image, they're asking for their image with one thing changed. And that's a fundamentally different contract than generation. In generation, if the model takes some creative liberty, that's often fine, maybe even welcome. In editing, every unrequested change is a failure, even if the result is technically a beautiful image.

And the reason this is hard is that the easiest way for a model to make an edit look good is to just regenerate everything. You ask it to change the color of a jacket, and it gives you a jacket in the new color, but now the person's face is slightly different, the lighting shifted, the texture of the wall behind them got smoothed out. Each of those drifts might be subtle, but humans are incredibly sensitive to them, especially on faces and on anything they have a memory of. If it's a photo of your kid, you notice immediately that it's not quite your kid anymore.

So faithfulness is really about preserving the identity of everything you didn't ask to change: the geometry, the lighting, the fine texture, the camera characteristics. And I'd argue that's actually where most of the difficulty in editing lives. Getting the requested change right is in some sense the easy part. Getting the model to leave everything else alone, while still integrating the change so it looks like it belongs in that scene, is the real problem. Because those two goals pull against each other. A perfectly faithful model that changes nothing is useless, and a model that changes freely isn't editing anymore.

The other thing I'd say is that faithfulness compounds. People rarely do one edit. They do five or ten in a row, and if each step introduces a little drift, by the end you've lost the image. So if you want editing to be a real workflow rather than a one-shot demo, preservation has to be close to lossless.

r001.rationale: It says subtle facial changes are immediately noticeable and can make a photo of someone’s child feel like it is “not quite your kid anymore,” directly linking slight facial drift to lost identity.

astra-6.text:
Because with editing, the input image is already telling you a lot about what the user wants. They’re not asking you to generate a new image that’s vaguely similar; they’re asking you to make a particular change to this image. So if you change someone’s shirt, you want their face, their pose, and the background to stay the same. Even if the result looks beautiful, if it changes the person’s identity, it hasn’t really fulfilled the request.

That’s what makes editing a different challenge from generation. You need the flexibility to make a meaningful change, but also the control to preserve everything that shouldn’t change. And that preservation is a big part of what makes an editing system useful—you can build on an image you care about without losing the things you liked about it.

r001.rationale: The response says the face should stay the same and that changing identity fails the request, but it does not explain that even slight inaccuracies in identity-defining facial details can noticeably undermine identity preservation.

sol-6.1.text:
When you edit an image, you usually want to change one particular thing while keeping everything else intact. You might want to change someone’s shirt, but preserve their face, their pose, the background, and the lighting. A result can look very realistic and still fail as an edit if it changes all those other details.

So faithfulness matters because the input image is part of the specification. The challenge is to give the model enough freedom to make the requested change, while constraining it to preserve the things you didn’t ask to change. That’s what makes editing useful and predictable.

r001.rationale: The response says to preserve the person’s face, but does not explain that even slight inaccuracies in identity-defining facial details can noticeably undermine identity preservation.
